write.desc: This topic teaches the set and function language that analysis is written in, from basic notation and set operations through indexed unions and intersections to images, preimages, injections, surjections, bijections and inverses. The aim is that the learner can prove set identities and function properties directly from the definitions.

points.name: Sets, elements and set notation
points.what: Read and write sets using roster notation, set-builder notation {x in A : P(x)} and interval notation such as [a,b), (a,infinity), and recognise the empty set and the standard sets N, Z, Q, R. Tell an element (x in A) apart from a subset.
outside: statements and the meaning of 'x is in A' as a statement that is true or false

points.name: Subsets, set equality and double inclusion
points.what: State A is a subset of B as 'for every x, if x in A then x in B', prove a subset claim by taking an arbitrary element, and prove two sets are equal by showing each is a subset of the other. Know that the empty set is a subset of every set (vacuous truth).
outside: implication and the vacuously true case
proving a 'for all' statement by taking an arbitrary element

points.name: Union, intersection, difference and complement
points.what: Define union, intersection, difference A \ B and complement relative to a universal set through 'or', 'and' and 'not', and compute them for simple sets and intervals. Recognise disjoint sets.

points.name: Proving set identities and De Morgan's laws for sets
points.what: Prove set identities such as distributive laws and De Morgan's laws for sets by double inclusion, translating each membership statement into logic. Disprove a false identity with a concrete counterexample.
outside: disproving a statement by a counterexample

points.name: Cartesian products
points.what: Understand ordered pairs and the product A x B, picture subsets of R x R, and prove simple facts about products such as A x (B union C) = (A x B) union (A x C).

points.name: Indexed families, indexed unions and intersections
points.what: Read an indexed family {A_i : i in I} over any index set and the definitions: x is in the union exactly when there exists i with x in A_i, and x is in the intersection exactly when x in A_i for all i. Translate between the set notation and the quantified statement in both directions.
outside: the quantifiers 'for all' and 'there exists' with explicit domains

points.name: Working with indexed unions and intersections
points.what: Compute and prove facts such as: the union of [1/n, 1] over n is (0,1], the intersection of (0,1/n) is empty, the intersection of [0,1/n] is {0}, and nested intervals behave this way. Prove De Morgan's laws for indexed families and handle the case of an empty intersection.
outside: proving 'there exists' by producing a witness

points.name: Functions: domain, codomain, graph and restriction
points.what: Understand a function f: A -> B as a rule assigning to each element of A exactly one element of B, its graph as a subset of A x B, when two functions are equal, and the restriction of f to a subset of its domain. Know that range and codomain differ, and that a relation is any subset of a product (mentioned only).

points.name: Image and preimage of a set
points.what: Define the image f(C) and the preimage f^{-1}(D) of sets and compute them for functions such as x^2 and sin on intervals. Know that the preimage is defined for every function, with or without an inverse.
outside: proving 'there exists' by producing a witness

points.name: Images and preimages with unions, intersections and complements
points.what: Prove that preimages preserve unions, intersections (including indexed ones) and complements, that images preserve unions, and that f(C intersect D) is only a subset of f(C) intersect f(D), with a counterexample showing equality can fail. Prove C is a subset of f^{-1}(f(C)) and f(f^{-1}(D)) is a subset of D.
outside: disproving a statement by a counterexample

points.name: Injective, surjective and bijective functions
points.what: State the definitions with quantifiers, prove a given function is injective (assume f(x)=f(y), show x=y) or surjective (given y, find x), and disprove each with a counterexample. See how the same rule can change these properties when the domain or codomain changes.
outside: turning a quantified statement into the skeleton of its proof

points.name: Composition of functions
points.what: Define g o f when the codomain of f fits the domain of g, know composition is associative but not commutative, and prove that compositions of injections are injective and of surjections are surjective, together with the partial converses (if g o f is injective then f is).

points.name: Inverse functions
points.what: Prove that f has an inverse function exactly when it is bijective, characterise the inverse by g o f = id and f o g = id, and get bijections by restricting the domain (square root, arcsin). Keep the inverse function apart from the preimage notation f^{-1}(D), which exists for every function.
